summary: Describes BagIt, a set of directory layout conventions for storing and transferring digital content. A bag holds descriptive metadata tags and a payload of files, without needing to know what the files contain.

plainLanguage.summary: A bag is a box with a packing list and your stuff. Anyone can open it and check nothing is missing.

questions: how to validate a bagit bag
subtitle: A simple directory format for packaging digital content with integrity checking.

tldr.problem: Digital archives and libraries need a straightforward way to package files for storage and transfer, with built-in integrity checking and metadata, but without requiring specialized tools or knowledge of file contents.
tldr.mechanism: BagIt defines a hierarchical directory structure with a payload directory for files, manifest files listing checksums, tag files for metadata, and optional fetch files for downloading remote content. Any tool can read and verify a bag using standard checksums.
tldr.outcome: BagIt became widely adopted in digital preservation by the Library of Congress, Dryad Data Repository, university libraries, and many others. The format is simple, requires no serialization, and allows direct filesystem access while maintaining strong integrity assurances.

today: RFC 8493 is an Informational document published in October 2018. BagIt remains widely adopted in digital preservation, with implementations in Python, Ruby, Java, Perl, PHP, and other languages. The Library of Congress, Stanford, NYU, Purdue, Ghent University, and numerous other institutions use BagIt for their archival workflows. The specification is stable and not expected to change in the near future.

sections.title: The Problem: Packaging Digital Content
sections.content:
Libraries, archives, and data repositories manage vast collections of digital files. They need to store these files reliably, transfer them between systems, and verify that nothing corrupted in transit. Traditional approaches use serialized formats like TAR, ZIP, or MIME, which bundle everything into a single file. But this creates problems: you must extract the entire archive to access a single file, size limits and memory constraints are possible, and the archive itself becomes a point of failure.

BagIt takes a different approach. Instead of serialization, it defines a set of directory structure conventions—a "bag" is just a directory on the filesystem. The payload files live as regular files in a data/ subdirectory, accessible with any tool. Metadata and checksums go in simple text files. No special knowledge of file contents is required; the format is format-agnostic.

The name comes from the archival phrase "bag it and tag it"—enclose your content and attach labels describing it.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of zipping everything into one file, BagIt keeps files as separate files with a packing list. That way you can access any file without unpacking everything.

sections.title: Structure: What Makes a Bag
sections.content:
Every BagIt bag is a directory containing these essential elements:

1. The bag declaration (bagit.txt): Two required lines that identify the bag version and the character encoding of metadata files.

2. The data directory: A subdirectory named data/ containing the payload files. This can have any internal structure of subdirectories. The payload files are opaque octet streams; BagIt does not interpret their contents.

3. Payload manifest(s): One or more files named manifest-algorithm.txt (e.g., manifest-sha256.txt) that list every payload file with its checksum. A bag can have multiple manifests using different algorithms for redundancy or future-proofing.

A bag MAY also contain:

4. Tag manifest(s): Files named tagmanifest-algorithm.txt that list checksums for all tag files (but not payload files), allowing verification of metadata integrity.

5. Bag metadata (bag-info.txt): Human-readable metadata such as source organization, contact information, external descriptions, bagging date, and a Payload-Oxum field showing total octet count and file count as a quick sanity check.

6. Fetch file (fetch.txt): A list of URLs to fetch before the bag can be validated. Allows bags to be transferred with "holes" that the receiver fills in.

7. Custom tag files: Any other tag files the creator wants to include.
sections.plainLanguage: A bag has a label file saying what version it is, a data folder with files, and a list of what each file's checksum should be. It can also have other labels like who packed it and where to download missing files.

sections.title: Validation and Completeness
sections.content:
BagIt defines two levels of bag quality:

Complete: A bag is complete if every required element is present, every file listed in every manifest exists, every payload file is listed in every payload manifest, and every optional file listed in a tag manifest exists. Completeness is about structure and presence.

Valid: A complete bag is valid if every checksum in every manifest has been successfully verified against the actual file contents. Validation requires computing hashes and comparing them.

The validation process is straightforward: for each line in a manifest, compute the specified checksum of the file and compare it to the hex-encoded value in the manifest. If all match, the bag is valid. The process requires no knowledge of what the files contain—they are just octet streams to hash.

Implementations MUST support SHA-256 and SHA-512 algorithms and SHOULD default to SHA-512 for new bags. They SHOULD also support MD5 and SHA-1 for backwards compatibility.
sections.plainLanguage: First you check that all the files on the list are really there (complete). Then you recompute all the checksums and see if they match the list (valid).

sections.title: Fetch Files: Bags with Remote Payloads
sections.content:
A fetch file allows a bag to be transmitted without its complete payload. Each line in fetch.txt specifies a URL, an optional file size in octets, and a filepath relative to the bag root.

This is useful when payload files are large or distributed. For example, a museum collection might be managed on a server, but the bag (metadata, manifests) is sent separately. The receiver's tool reads the fetch file, downloads each URL, places the file in the correct payload location, and then validates the bag. Any file listed in a fetch file MUST also be listed in the payload manifest.

Fetch files introduce security considerations: a bag's fetch file might point to untrusted hosts, or the file size might not match the actual download. Implementations should verify file sizes and use strong checksums to protect against spoofing. However, checksums alone do not provide cryptographic security against active attacks; that requires digital signatures, which are out of scope for BagIt.
sections.plainLanguage: If you don't want to send the actual files (they're too big), you can give the receiver a URL to download each one from. The bag tells them what the file should look like when they download it.

sections.title: Interoperability and Practical Considerations
sections.content:
BagIt is designed to work across operating systems and filesystems, but cross-platform complications exist.

Filename case sensitivity: Some filesystems (Unix) are case-sensitive, while others (Windows NTFS, macOS HFS+) are case-insensitive. A manifest listing both data/file.txt and data/FILE.txt might cause one to overwrite the other on case-insensitive systems. Implementations SHOULD warn when bags contain files differing only in case.

Unicode normalization: Different systems normalize Unicode filenames differently. macOS HFS+ always decomposes characters, while Windows treats filenames as opaque byte sequences. A file named "Núñez" on one system may not match the same-looking name on another. Implementations SHOULD apply the same normalization form to both filesystem and manifest names before comparing them.

Path separators: BagIt specifies that only forward slashes ('/') may appear in manifest and fetch.txt files. Windows implementations MUST translate between Windows backslashes and forward slashes.

Reserved names: Windows reserves names like CON, PRN, AUX, NUL, COM1–COM9, and LPT1–LPT9. Implementations SHOULD warn or prevent creation of bags with payload files using these names.

The Library of Congress publishes a conformance test suite to help implementers validate their BagIt tools across these scenarios.
sections.plainLanguage: Macs, Windows, and Linux handle filenames differently—case matters on Linux but not Windows, special characters behave differently, etc. BagIt tools need to be careful about these differences so bags work everywhere.

sections.title: Integrity, Not Security
sections.content:
A critical point: BagIt provides integrity assurance against accidental corruption, not security against active attacks. Checksums detect bit rot, transmission errors, and accidental file modifications. But they do not authenticate the origin of a bag or prove an attacker did not modify it.

For example, an attacker could modify a payload file and recompute its checksum in the manifest. The bag would validate successfully. To prevent this, organizations needing security SHOULD add digital signatures outside the scope of BagIt—sign the manifest file with a private key so only authorized parties can modify it.

Similarly, directory traversal attacks are a risk: a maliciously crafted manifest might list paths like "../../../outside/" or "/etc/passwd" in an attempt to cause a naive implementation to write files outside the bag. Implementations MUST validate paths to ensure they stay within the bag directory, and SHOULD have test suites to guard against this.

The fetch file also presents attack surface: URLs might point to malicious hosts, and file size fields can be spoofed. Implementations should verify actual file sizes do not exceed declared sizes and should use strong checksums for all files.
sections.plainLanguage: Checksums catch accidental mistakes but not deliberate tampering. If you need to prevent someone from changing files, you need to add digital signatures or other security measures on top.
